label: AQ 0013
title: The workflow that kept its promises

questions.q: So should the agent never replace the workflow?
questions.a: It can, once every promise lives in code and passes its tests. Then the agent decides only what was never promised, like how to compare messy offers. Anthropic's advice fits: workflows give “predictability and consistency for well-defined tasks”, agents suit work that needs flexibility.

teach.title: How it works: replacing a workflow safely

questions.q: Why does the agent score higher at all?
questions.a: Find out which cases it wins. If it wins on messy orders the fixed steps handled badly, that's real value worth keeping, inside the fence.

teach.title: How it works: replacing a workflow safely

questions.q: What else does the switch cost?
questions.a: Anthropic's guide warns that agentic systems often trade speed and cost for better results. Compare cost per correct order, not just the score.

teach.title: How it works: replacing a workflow safely

questions.q: Why can't a benchmark built from the workflow's own past runs see its guarantees?
questions.a: The workflow never broke them, so no case in the data shows a promise being broken, or even tempts the agent to break one.

questions.q: What is pass^k, and why does it suit a guarantee?
questions.a: The chance that all k tries at the same task succeed. A guarantee has to hold every time, so you care about the worst run, not the average.

questions.q: Put the safe switch in order.
questions.a: List the promises, move each into code, test them pass or fail with tempting cases, run the agent alongside the workflow, and delete the workflow last.
